lines.text:
A Home Away from Home — The Hotel Experience

A hotel is a temporary residence — a place where strangers become guests and service replaces routine. Whether a budget roadside stop or a five-star resort, every hotel operates on the same principle: anticipate what the traveller needs before they ask for it.

The experience begins in the lobby. A chandelier hangs from the ceiling. A sofa and a vase of flowers create an impression of domestic comfort. The front desk is the operational centre: a receptionist greets arrivals, issues a key card, and explains the hotel's facilities. A bell sits on the counter for attention. A luggage cart holds suitcases. A doorman opens the entrance for arriving guests. A bellhop carries bags to the room.

Room types range from a single room to a double room, a suite, and — at the top — a penthouse. Each room contains a bed with a pillow and a blanket, a nightstand with a lamp, and a closet for hanging clothes. A safe stores valuables. A mini bar offers drinks and snacks at a premium. An iron and a hair dryer are standard amenities. The bathroom includes a bathtub or a shower, a towel, a robe, slippers, soap, shampoo, a mirror, a sink, and a toilet. A balcony offers a view — of the city, the sea, or the garden.

Services define the hotel's quality. Room service delivers meals at any hour. A wake up call replaces the alarm clock. A concierge arranges restaurants, tickets, and transport. A valet parks the car. Housekeeping cleans and restocks the room daily. A breakfast buffet is often included. A shuttle connects the hotel to the airport or city centre. A tour desk arranges excursions. Wifi is expected. Parking is either complimentary or charged.

Facilities extend beyond the room. A swimming pool — indoor or outdoor — is the most requested amenity. A gym provides exercise equipment. A spa offers treatments. A restaurant serves meals. A bar provides evening drinks. A rooftop terrace offers panoramic views. A garden creates outdoor space. A conference room and a business center serve corporate guests. A laundry service handles clothing.

The infrastructure is invisible but essential. An elevator connects floors. A hallway leads to numbered doors. An ice machine and a vending machine serve late-night needs. The checkout process — reviewing charges, returning the key card, settling the bill — concludes the stay.

What separates a forgettable hotel from a memorable one is rarely the thread count or the lobby design. It is whether the guest felt noticed — whether someone remembered their name, anticipated their request, or simply smiled at the right moment. Hospitality, at its best, is the art of making a stranger feel expected.

lines.text: Tag questions repeat the auxiliary from the main clause. 'Has' (as a main verb meaning 'possesses') uses 'doesn't' in the tag: 'has good facilities, doesn't it?' If 'has' were an auxiliary: 'The hotel has been renovated, hasn't it?' Match the auxiliary: present simple → 'does/doesn't'; 'has' as auxiliary → 'has/hasn't.'

lines.text: 'Accommodation' is uncountable in British English — never *'an accommodation' or *'accommodations' (though American English sometimes uses the plural). Use: 'accommodation', 'some accommodation', 'the accommodation.' Similar: 'luggage' (not *a luggage), 'furniture' (not *a furniture), 'information' (not *an information).

lines.text: 'Tell' + direct object (no 'to'): 'told us.' 'Say' + 'to': 'said to us.' Never *'told to us.' Pattern: tell + person + that-clause: 'She told us that...' Say + that-clause: 'She said that...' Say + to + person: 'She said to us that...' The person after 'tell' is always a direct object.

lines.text: 'Despite' + noun/gerund (no clause): 'despite the rain', 'despite being tired.' 'Although' + full clause: 'although it was raining.' Never *'despite + subject + verb.' 'In spite of' follows the same rule as 'despite': 'in spite of the rain.' This is a persistent B2 error — the two structures look interchangeable but have different grammar.

lines.text: 'Every' + singular noun + singular verb: 'every room has.' 'All' + plural noun + plural verb: 'all rooms have.' 'Each' + singular: 'each room has.' Never *'every rooms' — 'every' is always followed by a singular noun. Compare: 'every guest is welcome' vs. 'all guests are welcome.'

lines.text: Stars indicate quality: 1★ = basic, 2★ = standard, 3★ = comfortable, 4★ = superior, 5★ = luxury. Rating systems vary by country. 'Boutique hotel' = a small, stylish, individually designed hotel (usually 4-5★). 'Budget hotel' = affordable, no-frills accommodation.

lines.text: UK: tipping is not required but appreciated (£1-2 for porters, £1/night for housekeeping). US: tipping is expected — $1-2/bag for bellhops, $2-5/night for housekeeping, left on the pillow or bedside table. Always in cash.

lines.text: 'B&B' (bed and breakfast) = a small, family-run guesthouse. 'Hostel' = budget accommodation with shared dormitory rooms (popular with young travellers). 'Airbnb' = a platform for renting private homes or rooms. 'Self-catering' = accommodation with a kitchen (you cook for yourself).

lines.text: Hotels use 'complimentary' instead of 'free' — it sounds more elegant. 'Complimentary breakfast', 'complimentary Wi-Fi', 'complimentary toiletries'. Don't confuse with 'complementary' (= completing something, e.g. complementary colours). Different spelling, different meaning!
